cards.front: Which two tissues force the body to make new glucose during a fast, and why does each depend on glucose?
cards.back: The brain, which runs almost entirely on glucose until a fast lasts several days and ketones take over part of the load, and red blood cells, which have no mitochondria and run on glucose alone.
cards.quote: Your brain runs almost entirely on glucose until a fast lasts several days and ketones take over part of the load

cards.front: After glycogen runs low in a fast, the liver (with help from the kidney cortex) manufactures fresh glucose that keeps fasting blood glucose at about {{c1::70–100 mg/dL}}.
cards.quote: blood sugar stays in its narrow lane (about 70–100 mg/dL fasting)

cards.front: How do glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis share the job of supplying blood glucose over the first days of a fast?
cards.back: Glycogen breakdown supplies most glucose in the first hours, with gluconeogenesis already contributing. Gluconeogenesis rises as glycogen falls; after glycogen runs low within a day or two, new glucose holds blood sugar up.
cards.why: It is a gradual handover, not a sudden switch.
cards.quote: gluconeogenesis rises as glycogen falls, and the two share the load until glycogen runs low within a day or two

cards.front: Name the three classes of gluconeogenic precursor and where each enters the pathway.
cards.back: Lactate: converted to pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase. Glucogenic amino acids (alanine chief among them; glutamine): lose nitrogen, enter at pyruvate or citric acid cycle intermediates that become oxaloacetate. Glycerol: enters as DHAP.
cards.quote: Lactate comes back from hard-working muscle and red cells; lactate dehydrogenase converts it to pyruvate.
cards.section: Where the carbons come from

cards.front: The kidney's main gluconeogenic amino acid is {{c1::glutamine}}.
cards.back: Alanine is the chief one overall.
cards.quote: plus glutamine, the kidney's main gluconeogenic amino acid
cards.section: Where the carbons come from

cards.front: Does an enzyme set the direction a metabolic reaction runs? If not, what does?
cards.back: No. An enzyme speeds a reaction both ways. ΔG under cellular conditions sets the direction: near zero, the step is near equilibrium and reversible; large and negative, it runs one way in practice.
cards.quote: An enzyme speeds a reaction both ways; it does not pick a direction.
cards.section: Three cliffs: why the pathway can't just run backward

cards.front: Which three glycolytic steps are far from equilibrium, and roughly what is each one's ΔG inside the cell?
cards.back: Hexokinase, about −33 kJ/mol; phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1), about −22 kJ/mol; pyruvate kinase, about −17 kJ/mol. The other seven steps are near equilibrium and shared with gluconeogenesis.
cards.why: Classic estimates from red blood cell metabolite levels; textbooks differ by a few kJ/mol.
cards.quote: Seven of glycolysis's ten steps are near equilibrium, and gluconeogenesis shares those seven enzymes.
cards.section: Three cliffs: why the pathway can't just run backward

cards.front: Using the rule of thumb that at body temperature every ~6 kJ/mol of ΔG is a tenfold change in the product/reactant ratio, by about how much must that ratio shift to bring a step with ΔG = −18 kJ/mol to equilibrium?
cards.back: 18 / 6 = 3 tenfold steps, so 10³ ≈ 1000-fold. Running the step backward would take more still.
cards.quote: At body temperature, every 6 kJ/mol or so of ΔG is a tenfold change in the ratio of products to reactants.
cards.section: Three cliffs: why the pathway can't just run backward

cards.front: Why can a liver cell not simply run pyruvate kinase backward by piling up pyruvate and ATP?
cards.back: Only in principle: just reaching equilibrium would need about a 650-fold shift in the product/reactant ratio (about 400,000-fold for hexokinase). No cell can hold ATP, ADP and sugar phosphates that far from normal.
cards.quote: Just to bring pyruvate kinase to equilibrium the cell would have to shift that ratio about 650-fold
cards.section: Three cliffs: why the pathway can't just run backward

cards.front: How does gluconeogenesis get past the two glycolytic steps where ATP put a phosphate on (hexokinase/glucokinase and PFK-1)?
cards.back: It does not hand the phosphate back to ADP. It cuts it off with water: glucose-6-phosphatase and FBPase-1 hydrolyze the phosphate, downhill by about −14 and −16 kJ/mol (standard values).
cards.quote: gluconeogenesis does not hand the phosphate back to ADP; it cuts it off with water.
cards.section: Three cliffs: why the pathway can't just run backward

cards.front: Turning pyruvate back into PEP with one ATP spent is uphill by about +31 kJ/mol under standard conditions. A second high-energy phosphate is worth about 30.5 kJ/mol. What is the standard ΔG with both, and how does it behave in the liver?
cards.back: +31 − 30.5 ≈ +0.5 kJ/mol (the lesson rounds to ≈ +1): about even under standard conditions, and comfortably downhill in the liver. The two phosphates are an ATP at pyruvate carboxylase and a GTP at PEPCK.
cards.quote: even with one ATP spent, turning pyruvate back into PEP is uphill by about 31 kJ/mol under standard conditions
cards.section: Three cliffs: why the pathway can't just run backward

cards.front: If glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are both downhill in the liver, what decides which one runs?
cards.back: Regulation. Every step runs downhill in the direction it is used, so thermodynamics no longer picks the direction; the cell chooses with controls at each of the three enzyme pairs.
cards.quote: With both pathways downhill, thermodynamics no longer picks the direction; the cell has to choose, by regulation.
cards.section: Three cliffs: why the pathway can't just run backward

cards.front: Pyruvate carboxylase: where does it work, what reaction does it catalyze, what cofactor carries the CO₂, and what activates it?
cards.back: In the mitochondrion it adds CO₂ to pyruvate to make oxaloacetate, spending one ATP. Biotin carries the CO₂. Acetyl-CoA activates it, the signal that fuel is plentiful so the cell should make glucose rather than burn pyruvate.
cards.quote: Inside the mitochondrion, pyruvate carboxylase adds CO₂ to pyruvate to make oxaloacetate, spending one ATP.
cards.section: Bypass 1: pyruvate to PEP, across two compartments

cards.front: Why is oxaloacetate exported from the mitochondrion as malate (from pyruvate or alanine) rather than as itself?
cards.back: Oxaloacetate has no transporter across the inner mitochondrial membrane. It is reduced to malate, exported on the malate–α-ketoglutarate carrier, and oxidized back to oxaloacetate in the cytosol, carrying reducing power with it. From lactate it can leave as aspartate instead.
cards.quote: oxaloacetate has no transporter across the inner mitochondrial membrane
cards.section: Bypass 1: pyruvate to PEP, across two compartments

cards.front: A liver cell makes glucose from lactate rather than from alanine. How is oxaloacetate likely to leave the mitochondrion, and why?
cards.back: As aspartate rather than malate. Reverse GAPDH needs one cytosolic NADH per three-carbon unit, and lactate dehydrogenase already made that NADH in the cytosol, so the malate route's NADH delivery is not needed.
cards.why: From pyruvate or alanine the NADH must come out of the mitochondrion, and malate brings it.
cards.quote: From lactate, lactate dehydrogenase already made the NADH in the cytosol, so oxaloacetate can leave as aspartate instead.
cards.section: Bypass 1: pyruvate to PEP, across two compartments

cards.front: Why does gluconeogenesis add a CO₂ to pyruvate only for PEPCK to remove it one step later?
cards.back: No single animal enzyme turns pyruvate into PEP. Pyruvate carboxylase spends ATP to attach CO₂, storing energy in oxaloacetate; PEPCK's decarboxylation is downhill and, with a GTP, pays for PEP. CO₂ is a thermodynamic lever.
cards.quote: The CO₂ is the handle that lets two enzymes, in two compartments, share the job.
cards.section: Bypass 1: pyruvate to PEP, across two compartments

cards.front: Why can even-chain fatty acids not supply net glucose?
cards.back: Every PEP made uses up one oxaloacetate. Acetyl-CoA joins one oxaloacetate to enter the citric acid cycle; over a turn two carbons leave as CO₂ and exactly one oxaloacetate comes back. Net oxaloacetate gain is zero.
cards.quote: over a turn, two carbons leave as CO₂ and exactly one oxaloacetate comes back
cards.section: Why fat can't become sugar

cards.front: Why can humans not turn fatty-acid-derived acetyl-CoA back into pyruvate for gluconeogenesis?
cards.back: Pyruvate dehydrogenase releases CO₂ in a step so far downhill that it runs one way only, from pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.
cards.quote: Pyruvate dehydrogenase releases CO₂ in a step so far downhill that it runs one way only
cards.section: Why fat can't become sugar

cards.front: Carbon-labeled palmitate is given to a fasting subject, and some label appears in blood glucose. A second researcher concludes that fat makes net glucose. Is that right? Explain the label.
cards.back: No. The label appears because the citric acid cycle shuffles atoms between acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate, not because oxaloacetate is gained. Each acetyl-CoA consumes and returns one oxaloacetate, so net glucose from even-chain fatty acids stays zero.
cards.why: Rests on the no-net-oxaloacetate rule; label tracing measures atom exchange, not net flux.
cards.quote: Carbon label from a fatty acid can still turn up in glucose, because the cycle shuffles atoms
cards.section: Why fat can't become sugar

cards.front: Could a 17-carbon (odd-chain) fatty acid supply any net glucose in a human liver? Why?
cards.back: Yes, the exception. Its final three-carbon unit, propionyl-CoA, can be routed through succinyl-CoA to oxaloacetate. The rest of the chain yields acetyl-CoA, which gives none.
cards.quote: The one exception is odd-chain fatty acids, whose final three-carbon propionyl-CoA can be routed through succinyl-CoA to oxaloacetate.
cards.section: Why fat can't become sugar

cards.front: A germinating oil seed turns stored fatty acids into sugar, which a human liver cannot do. What must the plant have, and how does it get around the human block?
cards.back: Two glyoxylate-cycle enzymes. They let acetyl-CoA skip the citric acid cycle's two CO₂-releasing steps, so carbon is kept and oxaloacetate is gained net, which can feed PEPCK. Humans and other vertebrates lack these enzymes.
cards.quote: two glyoxylate-cycle enzymes let acetyl-CoA skip the cycle's two CO₂-releasing steps, giving them a net gain of oxaloacetate
cards.section: Why fat can't become sugar

cards.front: During a long fast, stored triglyceride (glycerol plus three palmitates) is mobilized. Which part can become blood glucose, and where does it enter?
cards.back: Only the glycerol backbone. It enters as DHAP, above PEP, so it needs no oxaloacetate. The even-chain palmitates give acetyl-CoA, which yields no net oxaloacetate and so no net glucose.
cards.quote: Of the fat you actually carry, only the glycerol backbone can become sugar.
cards.section: Why fat can't become sugar

cards.front: What inhibits and what activates fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase-1)?
cards.back: Inhibited by AMP and by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate; activated by citrate.
cards.quote: It is a major regulated step, inhibited by AMP and by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and activated by citrate.
cards.section: Bypasses 2 and 3, and why muscle can't share

cards.front: FBPase-1 hydrolysis is downhill by about 16 kJ/mol (standard). PFK-1 is downhill by about 14, so handing the phosphate back to ADP would be uphill by about 14. What is the gap, and what does it represent?
cards.back: 16 + 14 ≈ 30 kJ/mol, about one ATP's worth: the ATP PFK-1 spent, which gluconeogenesis never gets back. The cost is a refund given up, not a payment.
cards.quote: The gap, about 30 kJ/mol, is one ATP's worth: the ATP that PFK-1 spent, which gluconeogenesis never gets back.
cards.section: Bypasses 2 and 3, and why muscle can't share

cards.front: Where in the cell does glucose-6-phosphatase work, and which tissues express the glucose-releasing form (G6Pase-α)?
cards.back: In the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum; the T1 transporter carries glucose-6-phosphate in. Liver, kidney cortex and, to a lesser degree, small intestine express G6Pase-α.
cards.quote: Only liver, kidney cortex and, to a lesser degree, the small intestine express the glucose-releasing form, G6Pase-α.
cards.section: Bypasses 2 and 3, and why muscle can't share

cards.front: Why can skeletal muscle not release its glycogen into the blood as glucose, and what does it export instead?
cards.back: Muscle lacks G6Pase-α, so it cannot remove the phosphate from glucose-6-phosphate. It uses its glycogen locally and, in hard work, ships out lactate it makes faster than it can use.
cards.quote: Muscle does not, so it cannot send its glycogen into the blood as glucose
cards.section: Bypasses 2 and 3, and why muscle can't share

cards.front: What does one glucose made from two pyruvates cost in ATP, GTP and NADH?
cards.back: 4 ATP + 2 GTP + 2 NADH. Pyruvate carboxylase 2 ATP, PEPCK 2 GTP, phosphoglycerate kinase 2 ATP, GAPDH 2 NADH; FBPase-1 and glucose-6-phosphatase cost nothing.
cards.quote: That is 4 ATP + 2 GTP + 2 NADH per glucose.
cards.section: The bill

cards.front: Why does counting only the four bypass enzymes undercount the ATP cost of gluconeogenesis?
cards.back: Two of the six high-energy phosphates are spent at a shared step: phosphoglycerate kinase run in reverse costs 1 ATP per pyruvate instead of making one.
cards.quote: Two of the six high-energy phosphates are spent at a shared step, which a count of only the bypass enzymes misses.
cards.section: The bill

cards.front: Glycolysis is downhill by about 85 kJ/mol under standard conditions. Gluconeogenesis spends four more high-energy phosphates than glycolysis returns, at about 30.5 kJ/mol each. What is the approximate standard ΔG of gluconeogenesis?
cards.back: Reverse glycolysis: +85. Extra push: 4 × 30.5 = 122. +85 − 122 ≈ −37 kJ/mol, so the coupled climb runs downhill.
cards.quote: Under standard conditions glycolysis is downhill by about 85 kJ/mol, so running it literally backward would be uphill by 85.
cards.section: The bill

cards.front: During hard exercise, five glucose molecules go around the Cori cycle (muscle to lactate, liver back to glucose). How many high-energy phosphates does the body lose overall, and who pays?
cards.back: Muscle banks 2 per glucose (10); the liver spends 6 per glucose (30). Net cost 5 × (6 − 2) = 20 high-energy phosphates, paid by the liver (in a fast, fueled largely by fat oxidation).
cards.quote: Each loop costs the body 4 high-energy phosphates, paid by the liver (in a fast, fueled largely by fat oxidation).
cards.section: The bill

cards.front: If glycolysis and gluconeogenesis ran at full speed in the same liver cell, how many high-energy phosphates would each turn waste, and at which enzyme pairs?
cards.back: Four per turn, released as heat: one at the glucose pair, one at the middle pair, and two at the pyruvate pair (an ATP and a GTP to make each PEP, minus one ATP back from pyruvate kinase).
cards.quote: Each turn wastes four high-energy phosphates: one at the glucose pair, one at the middle pair, and two at the pyruvate pair
cards.section: Downhill both ways: the switch at each pair

cards.front: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate {{c1::activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1}}; it is a regulator, not a pathway intermediate.
cards.back: 1,6 is the pathway; 2,6 is the regulator.
cards.quote: The best-known switch, fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP), works here, activating PFK-1 and inhibiting FBPase-1.
cards.section: Downhill both ways: the switch at each pair

cards.front: In the fed liver, how does insulin set the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme, and what follows?
cards.back: Insulin keeps it dephosphorylated, so the kinase (PFK-2) domain wins, fructose-2,6-bisphosphate rises, PFK-1 is activated, FBPase-1 is inhibited, and glycolysis runs.
cards.quote: In the fed liver, insulin keeps this bifunctional enzyme dephosphorylated, the kinase wins, F-2,6-BP rises, and glycolysis runs.
cards.section: Downhill both ways: the switch at each pair

cards.front: Glucagon rises at the start of a fast. Trace its effect from the receptor to FBPase-1 activity in a liver cell.
cards.back: FBPase-1 is released. Glucagon raises cAMP, activating PKA; PKA phosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme, the phosphatase (FBPase-2) wins, and F-2,6-BP falls. PFK-1 loses its activator and FBPase-1 loses its inhibitor.
cards.quote: Middle pair: PKA phosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme, the phosphatase wins, and F-2,6-BP falls.
cards.section: Downhill both ways: the switch at each pair

cards.front: What regulates liver pyruvate kinase?
cards.back: Shut off when PKA phosphorylates it; activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate; inhibited by ATP and alanine.
cards.quote: Liver pyruvate kinase is shut off when PKA phosphorylates it; fructose-1,6-bisphosphate activates it, and ATP and alanine inhibit it.
cards.section: Downhill both ways: the switch at each pair

cards.front: A mutation makes liver pyruvate kinase resistant to PKA phosphorylation. Predict glucose output from alanine in a fasting liver, and why.
cards.back: Glucose output falls and ATP is wasted. Pyruvate kinase stays more active, so newly made PEP is turned back into pyruvate, a futile cycle at the pyruvate pair, instead of climbing toward glucose.
cards.why: Normally PKA shuts off liver pyruvate kinase in a fast so new PEP is not recycled.
cards.quote: PKA shuts off liver pyruvate kinase, so new PEP is not turned back into pyruvate
cards.section: Downhill both ways: the switch at each pair

cards.front: How is the glucose pair (glucokinase versus glucose-6-phosphatase) controlled in the liver?
cards.back: Glucokinase's regulatory protein pulls glucokinase into the nucleus when glucose is low; over hours, insulin and glucagon change the amounts of the enzymes, shifting toward glucose-6-phosphatase in a fast.
cards.quote: The glucose pair is set by glucokinase's regulatory protein, which pulls glucokinase into the nucleus when glucose is low
cards.section: Downhill both ways: the switch at each pair

cards.front: A fasting liver is oxidizing fat. Explain how the products of fat oxidation favor gluconeogenesis at two different enzyme pairs.
cards.back: Fat oxidation keeps the liver's ATP high and raises acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate pair). High energy state keeps AMP low, which leaves FBPase-1 uninhibited (middle pair). Fasting and energy high point the same way.
cards.quote: burning fat supplies the liver's ATP and acetyl-CoA, and while its energy state stays high, AMP stays low, which also leaves FBPase-1 free
cards.section: Downhill both ways: the switch at each pair

cards.front: A drug selectively blocks the FBPase-2 domain of the bifunctional enzyme in liver. Predict fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels and glucose output during a fast.
cards.back: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate stays high, because the fasting signal (PKA favoring FBPase-2) can no longer lower it. FBPase-1 stays inhibited and PFK-1 stays active, so gluconeogenesis at the middle pair is held back and glucose output falls.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that F-2,6-BP activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1, and FBPase-2 breaks it down in a fast.
cards.quote: its two domains make (PFK-2) or break (FBPase-2) fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
cards.section: Downhill both ways: the switch at each pair

cards.front: A newborn with severe pyruvate carboxylase deficiency has lactic acidosis, hypoglycemia and high blood ammonia. Explain all three from the one missing enzyme.
cards.back: No oxaloacetate is made from pyruvate. Pyruvate piles up and becomes lactate (lactic acidosis); gluconeogenesis cannot start (hypoglycemia); and the same oxaloacetate, as aspartate, feeds the urea cycle, so nitrogen disposal falters (high ammonia).
cards.quote: because the same oxaloacetate also feeds the citric acid cycle and, as aspartate, the urea cycle
cards.section: When a bypass breaks

cards.front: A child lacks liver glucose-6-phosphatase (or its T1 transporter). Predict the findings after an overnight fast, and why.
cards.back: Severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and a liver swollen with glycogen. The liver can make glucose-6-phosphate from glycogen or gluconeogenesis but cannot release free glucose through its usual route. This is von Gierke disease (glycogen storage disease type I).
cards.quote: Von Gierke disease (glycogen storage disease type I) breaks Bypass 3.
cards.section: When a bypass breaks

cards.front: In type 2 diabetes, why does fasting blood glucose rise if no gluconeogenic enzyme is missing?
cards.back: Insulin no longer holds the liver's glucose output down. Much of the cause is extra fuel arriving from fat, which drives more gluconeogenesis.
cards.quote: Insulin no longer holds the liver's glucose output down, and fasting blood sugar rises; much of the cause is extra fuel arriving from fat.
cards.section: When a bypass breaks

cards.front: What does the alanine cycle carry from muscle to liver, and why is it needed?
cards.back: Muscle nitrogen, packaged on alanine, because muscle lacks the urea-cycle machinery to dispose of ammonia. In the liver alanine's carbon becomes pyruvate for gluconeogenesis. ALT runs the cycle; a rising serum ALT flags liver damage.
cards.quote: carries muscle nitrogen to the liver packaged on alanine, because muscle lacks the urea-cycle machinery to dispose of ammonia
cards.section: When a bypass breaks

cards.front: In insulin resistance, fat tissue releases more fatty acids. Fatty acids cannot become net glucose, yet they raise hepatic glucose output. How?
cards.back: They act as a regulator, not a substrate. Fatty acids raise liver acetyl-CoA, which activates pyruvate carboxylase and increases flux into gluconeogenesis; glucagon also stays high. Extra glycerol from fat adds substrate.
cards.quote: the fatty acids raise liver acetyl-CoA and so pyruvate carboxylase flux, and glucagon stays high
cards.section: Type 2 diabetes, PEPCK and metformin
